evidenceAudit.scope: Long-term outpatient care of adults with compensated and decompensated cirrhosis in India: diagnosis and staging (liver stiffness, clinically significant portal hypertension, MELD), treatment of the cause (alcohol, hepatitis B and C, MASLD), non-selective beta-blockers to prevent variceal bleeding and decompensation, variceal and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) surveillance, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) prevention, nutrition, vaccination and transplant referral. Built on NICE NG50, AASLD portal hypertension guidance (2023), a Baveno VII summary, BSG/BASL ascites (2020), AASLD/EASL hepatic encephalopathy (2014), the ICMR ALF/ACLF STW and NVHCP hepatitis B and C guidelines, because no Indian national cirrhosis guideline with doses could be opened.
findings: Transient elastography, hepatology referral, MELD every 6 months (12 or more = high risk), ultrasound with or without alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) every 6 months, endoscopy at diagnosis unless starting a beta-blocker and every 3 years if no varices, carvedilol first choice (start 6.25 mg/day) and propranolol second (start 40 mg twice daily), band ligation if beta-blockers not tolerated, carvedilol avoided in refractory ascites, selective SBP prophylaxis (ascitic protein 15 g/L or less, Child-Pugh above 9 or MELD above 16) checked against NICE NG50.

Carvedilol 12.5 mg/day target, dose reduction if systolic BP below 90 mmHg, switch to propranolol or nadolol if low BP limits carvedilol, endoscopy every 2 years (active disease), 3 years (controlled) or yearly (decompensated) when off beta-blockers, no screening endoscopy needed on a beta-blocker, band ligation every 2–4 weeks to obliteration then at 6 months and yearly, checked against the AASLD 2023 guidance (slide summary).

Clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH) defined as HVPG 10 mmHg or more and very likely with liver stiffness 25 kPa or more; beta-blockers to prevent decompensation in CSPH; screening endoscopy avoidable with liver stiffness below 20 kPa and platelets above 150 × 10⁹/L, checked against the Berzigotti summary of Baveno VII.

Spironolactone 100–400 mg and furosemide 40–160 mg, salt restriction, albumin after large-volume paracentesis and norfloxacin 400 mg or ciprofloxacin 500 mg daily SBP prophylaxis checked against BSG/BASL 2020 (recommendations 4.1–4.2, 2.8).

Lactulose titrated to 2–3 soft stools a day and rifaximin added after a second episode of hepatic encephalopathy checked against AASLD/EASL 2014 (recommendations 25–28); lactulose 20–30 mL 6-hourly and rifaximin 400 mg three times daily from the ICMR ALF/ACLF STW.

Energy 35–40 kcal/kg/day, protein 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day and a late-evening snack from the 2013 Clinical Liver Disease nutrition table; hepatitis B vaccination indicated in chronic liver disease (adult 1.0 mL doses at 0, 1–2 and 4–6 months) from Immunize.org and CDC.
unverifiedSections: INASL guidance and the full Baveno VII text were not opened; Baveno VII statements are from a published summary.
AASLD 2023 guidance was read as a slide summary.

Tenofovir, entecavir and sofosbuvir/velpatasvir doses for cirrhosis are taken from the NVHCP guidelines as recorded in the Chronic hepatitis B and C (India) topics; the NVHCP site blocks automated access, so they were not re-opened in this check.
The nutrition source is a 2013 review table for alcohol-related liver disease, applied here to cirrhosis of any cause.
Child-Pugh point thresholds are not stated because no opened source lists them; NICE NG50 uses Child-Pugh above 9 as a risk marker.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Cirrhosis is the end stage of chronic liver injury, in which fibrosis and regenerative nodules replace normal liver architecture. In India the commonest causes are alcohol, hepatitis B and C, and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD); autoimmune hepatitis and Wilson disease are less common. Its course has two phases. In compensated cirrhosis patients feel well for years, and the main determinant of outcome is portal hypertension: once the hepatic venous pressure gradient reaches 10 mmHg (clinically significant portal hypertension, CSPH) the risk of varices, ascites and death rises. Decompensation — ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy or jaundice — marks a sharp fall in survival. Long-term care therefore has four aims: remove the cause, lower portal pressure with carvedilol before decompensation, detect varices and HCC early, and prevent and treat complications while protecting nutrition and kidneys. Patients whose MELD score rises or who decompensate should be referred early for transplant assessment.
keyMechanisms: Hepatocyte injury activates stellate cells, which lay down collagen; fibrosis and nodules raise intrahepatic vascular resistance (portal hypertension).
Portal hypertension opens portosystemic collaterals (oesophageal and gastric varices) and causes splenomegaly with low platelets.
Splanchnic vasodilation lowers effective arterial volume, activating renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and causing sodium retention, ascites, hyponatraemia and hepatorenal syndrome.
Gut bacterial translocation and impaired immunity cause SBP and other infections; ammonia and inflammation cause hepatic encephalopathy.
Non-selective beta-blockers reduce portal inflow (cardiac output and splanchnic vasoconstriction); carvedilol also lowers intrahepatic resistance through alpha-1 blockade.
Ongoing injury and regeneration in a cirrhotic liver drive hepatocellular carcinoma, especially with hepatitis B.

symptoms: Confusion, sleep reversal or forgetfulness (hepatic encephalopathy)
physicalSigns: Spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, loss of body hair
redFlags: Gastrointestinal bleeding: emergency (see Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding topic)
Fever, abdominal pain or new confusion with ascites: diagnostic tap for SBP
New confusion: hepatic encephalopathy; look for infection, bleeding, constipation, sedatives
Rising creatinine or sodium below 125 mmol/L on diuretics
Rising MELD, jaundice or refractory ascites: transplant referral
New liver lesion on surveillance ultrasound or rising AFP

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Common in India: varices and splenomegaly with normal liver function and normal or only mildly raised liver stiffness; Doppler shows portal vein block in EHPVO.
Painful hepatomegaly and ascites with hepatic vein outflow obstruction on Doppler ultrasound or computed tomography (CT) venography.
Raised jugular venous pressure and high-protein ascites (SAAG 11 g/L or more with protein above 25 g/L); echocardiography settles it.
Fever and weight loss with exudative lymphocytic ascites (SAAG below 11 g/L); ascitic ADA and laparoscopy confirm.
Low SAAG ascites with malignant cytology; CT shows peritoneal deposits.
Generalised oedema with heavy proteinuria and low albumin; urine protein-creatinine ratio settles it.

clinicalManagement.title: Treat the cause
actions: Complete alcohol abstinence with de-addiction support (see Alcohol use disorder topic).
Antiviral treatment for hepatitis B or C (NVHCP); weight loss and metabolic control for MASLD.
Refer every patient with cirrhosis to a hepatologist (NICE 1.1.9).

clinicalManagement.title: Stage the disease
actions: Elastography, platelets, MELD; look for decompensation (NICE 1.2.2; Baveno summary).
CSPH likely (stiffness 25 kPa or more or varices): start a beta-blocker (Baveno summary).

clinicalManagement.title: Prevent bleeding and decompensation
actions: Titrate to heart rate and BP; reduce if systolic below 90 mmHg (AASLD).
Band ligation if beta-blockers are not tolerated or contraindicated (NICE 1.3.5).

clinicalManagement.title: Surveillance
actions: Ultrasound with or without AFP for HCC (NICE 1.2.4).
Endoscopy only if not on a beta-blocker: every 2–3 years, yearly if decompensated (NICE; AASLD).

clinicalManagement.title: Complications
actions: Ascites: salt restriction, spironolactone with or without furosemide; SBP prophylaxis in high-risk patients (BSG/BASL; NICE 1.3.7).
Hepatic encephalopathy: lactulose; add rifaximin after a recurrence (AASLD/EASL).

clinicalManagement.title: Nutrition and vaccination
actions: Energy 35–40 kcal/kg/day, protein 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day and a late-evening snack; do not restrict protein in encephalopathy.
Vaccinate against hepatitis B if non-immune (adult 3-dose schedule).

clinicalManagement.title: Refer for transplant assessment
clinicalManagement.timeframe: When MELD rises or after decompensation
actions: Specialist hepatology centre for complications or high risk (NICE 1.2.1).
Refractory ascites, recurrent encephalopathy, jaundice or HCC: transplant centre.

vignette.text: Mr R, a 52-year-old auto-rickshaw driver from Kanpur, drank about 90 g of alcohol daily for 20 years and stopped six months ago. He has no symptoms. Ultrasound for dyspepsia showed a nodular liver and a 14 cm spleen. Platelets are 98 × 10⁹/L, bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL, INR 1.3, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL and sodium 136 mmol/L. Liver stiffness is 31 kPa. He asks whether he needs a 'camera test' and whether there is anything he can do to stay well.

guidedApproach.title: Why portal pressure drives the outcome
guidedApproach.prompt: Why does a patient with normal liver function tests still carry a high risk?
guidedApproach.guidance:
Liver function tests measure hepatocyte injury and synthetic capacity, but they do not measure portal pressure. In cirrhosis, fibrosis and regenerative nodules distort the sinusoids and raise intrahepatic resistance, and blood flow into the portal system rises at the same time because the splanchnic vessels dilate. Once the hepatic venous pressure gradient reaches 10 mmHg, collaterals open, varices form, and the kidneys start retaining sodium. This threshold is called clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH). It is the strongest predictor of the first decompensation — ascites, variceal bleeding or encephalopathy — and decompensation, not the cirrhosis label itself, is what shortens life.
This is why the modern approach targets portal pressure early. Carvedilol lowers portal inflow and, through alpha-1 blockade, intrahepatic resistance. Started when CSPH is likely, it lowers the risk of decompensation as well as bleeding. Removing the cause (alcohol, hepatitis B or C) also lowers portal pressure over time and can lead to clinical recompensation.

guidedApproach.title: Recognising the patient who has changed
guidedApproach.prompt: Which findings at a routine visit mean the patient is no longer compensated?
guidedApproach.guidance: Most patients with compensated cirrhosis look well, so the task at each visit is to look for the transition. New ascites (weight gain, shifting dullness, leg swelling), any black stool or haematemesis, subtle encephalopathy (sleep reversal, poor concentration, a change noticed by family, asterixis) and new jaundice each signal decompensation and change the plan. Ask specifically about alcohol, over-the-counter painkillers and sedatives, because these precipitate decompensation and are common in India. Muscle wasting is easy to miss in a patient with ascites; check the temples and thighs and ask about protein intake. A patient who decompensates should be treated for the complication, reviewed for transplant, and have the precipitant identified.

guidedApproach.title: Staging without invasive tests
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you decide who needs endoscopy and who needs a beta-blocker?
guidedApproach.guidance: Elastography and the platelet count do most of the staging. A liver stiffness of 25 kPa or more makes CSPH very likely, so the patient gains from a beta-blocker whether or not varices are present; once a beta-blocker is started, a screening endoscopy does not change management. When stiffness is below 20 kPa and platelets are above 150 × 10⁹/L, the chance of varices needing treatment is low and endoscopy can be skipped, with yearly repeat testing. Patients between these groups, or those who cannot take a beta-blocker, need endoscopy to find medium or large varices, which then need either a beta-blocker or band ligation. Separately, every patient with cirrhosis needs an ultrasound, with or without AFP, every 6 months for HCC, and a MELD score every 6 months; a MELD of 12 or more marks high risk and should prompt specialist referral.

guidedApproach.title: Putting the long-term plan together
guidedApproach.prompt: What does a complete cirrhosis plan contain?
guidedApproach.guidance: A complete plan has five parts. First, treat the cause: support abstinence, start tenofovir or entecavir for hepatitis B, and treat hepatitis C with sofosbuvir and velpatasvir, because removing the cause can stop progression. Second, lower portal pressure: carvedilol starting at 6.25 mg a day and aiming for 12.5 mg a day, reducing the dose if systolic BP falls below 90 mmHg and avoiding it in refractory ascites. Third, surveillance: 6-monthly ultrasound and MELD, and endoscopy only when indicated. Fourth, prevent complications: salt restriction and diuretics for ascites, antibiotic prophylaxis only for high-risk patients, lactulose after an episode of encephalopathy with rifaximin added for recurrence, and strict avoidance of NSAIDs and sedatives. Fifth, protect the patient: adequate energy and protein with a late-evening snack, hepatitis B vaccination if non-immune, and early transplant referral when MELD rises or the patient decompensates.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 52-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis, abstinent for 6 months, has no symptoms. Liver stiffness is 31 kPa and platelets are 98 × 10⁹/L. He has never bled and has no ascites. His BP is 128/78 mmHg and pulse 84/min.
boardQuestions.question: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start carvedilol 6.25 mg daily
options.explanation: Correct. Stiffness of 25 kPa or more makes clinically significant portal hypertension very likely; carvedilol lowers the risk of decompensation and bleeding, so screening endoscopy would not change management.

options.text: Upper GI endoscopy before any treatment
options.explanation: Not needed first: when a beta-blocker is started because CSPH is likely, screening endoscopy does not change management (Baveno summary; NICE 1.2.6).

options.text: Prophylactic band ligation
options.explanation: Band ligation is for medium or large varices when beta-blockers are not tolerated or contraindicated; it does not prevent ascites or other decompensation.

options.text: Repeat elastography in 12 months
options.explanation: Watchful waiting is suitable only when stiffness is below 20 kPa with platelets above 150; this patient has CSPH.

options.text: Norfloxacin 400 mg daily
options.explanation: Antibiotic prophylaxis is for patients with ascites at high risk of SBP; he has no ascites.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Start carvedilol when liver stiffness or other findings show clinically significant portal hypertension, without waiting for endoscopy.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Liver stiffness 25 kPa or more: carvedilol, no screening endoscopy needed.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 60-year-old woman with hepatitis B cirrhosis on tenofovir has had carvedilol 12.5 mg daily for a year. She now has tense ascites needing large-volume paracentesis every 2 weeks despite maximum diuretics. Her BP is 86/54 mmHg and creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 1.5 mg/dL.
boardQuestions.question: What should be done with the carvedilol?

options.text: Continue at the same dose
options.explanation: Continuing exposes her to further hypotension and kidney injury; carvedilol should be avoided in refractory ascites (NICE 1.3.1).

options.text: Increase to 25 mg daily
options.explanation: Higher doses lower BP further and worsen renal perfusion; the target is 12.5 mg/day.

options.text: Reduce or stop it, and refer for transplant assessment
options.explanation: Correct. Systolic BP below 90 mmHg and refractory ascites with rising creatinine are reasons to reduce or stop the beta-blocker (AASLD; NICE 1.3.1), and refractory ascites is a transplant indication.

options.text: Switch to propranolol 80 mg twice daily
options.explanation: Switching to another non-selective beta-blocker at a higher dose does not solve hypotension and renal hypoperfusion.

options.text: Add midodrine and keep carvedilol
options.explanation: The cited sources do not support adding a vasoconstrictor to keep a beta-blocker going; they advise reducing or stopping it.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Recognise when a beta-blocker becomes harmful in advanced cirrhosis.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Systolic BP below 90 mmHg, refractory ascites or rising creatinine: reduce or stop the beta-blocker.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 48-year-old man with compensated hepatitis C cirrhosis was cured with sofosbuvir and velpatasvir (sustained virological response) 2 years ago. He does not drink alcohol, his MELD is 8, platelets are 140 × 10⁹/L and his last ultrasound was normal. He feels well and asks if he can stop his 6-monthly liver scans now that the virus has gone.
boardQuestions.question: What is the best advice?

options.text: Stop surveillance because he is cured
options.explanation: Cure lowers but does not remove HCC risk once cirrhosis is established.

options.text: Continue ultrasound with or without AFP every 6 months
options.explanation: Correct. NICE NG50 offers 6-monthly ultrasound with or without AFP to people with cirrhosis; the cirrhosis, not active virus, sets the risk.

options.text: Switch to a yearly CT scan
options.explanation: CT is not the recommended surveillance test and adds radiation and contrast exposure.

options.text: Check AFP alone every year
options.explanation: AFP alone misses many tumours; ultrasound is the core test.

options.text: Surveillance only if he develops symptoms
options.explanation: Symptomatic HCC is usually too advanced for curative treatment.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: HCC surveillance continues after viral cure in established cirrhosis.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Every patient with cirrhosis: ultrasound with or without AFP every 6 months.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 57-year-old woman with cirrhosis and ascites was admitted last month with overt hepatic encephalopathy triggered by constipation. She recovered on lactulose. Today she is oriented, passing two soft stools a day, and her family ask whether she should avoid eating dal and eggs to protect her brain.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most appropriate advice about diet?

options.text: Restrict protein to less than 0.5 g/kg/day
options.explanation: Protein restriction worsens sarcopenia and does not prevent encephalopathy.

options.text: Avoid all animal protein permanently
options.explanation: Unnecessary restriction worsens nutrition; protein needs are higher in cirrhosis.

options.text: Normal-to-high protein (1.2–1.5 g/kg/day), frequent meals and a late-evening snack, with lactulose continued
options.explanation: Correct. Cirrhosis is a catabolic state; adequate energy and protein with a late-evening snack prevent muscle loss, and lactulose continues as secondary prevention.

options.text: Fast overnight to rest the liver
options.explanation: Overnight fasting increases muscle breakdown in cirrhosis; a late-evening snack is advised.

options.text: Stop lactulose and start rifaximin alone
options.explanation: Rifaximin is added to lactulose after a recurrence, not substituted after one episode.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Nutrition in cirrhosis: do not restrict protein; prevent sarcopenia.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Protein 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day with a late-evening snack; keep lactulose after an episode of encephalopathy.

patientEducation: Avoid painkillers such as ibuprofen and diclofenac; paracetamol in normal doses is safer.
Seek care at once for black stools, vomiting blood, confusion, fever or abdominal swelling.
Take carvedilol daily even when well.
lifestyleAndDiet: Small frequent meals with adequate protein; late-evening snack; avoid fasting for long periods.
Salt restriction (no added salt) if ascites.
mdtReferrals: Transplant centre when MELD rises or after decompensation
dischargeCriteria: Outpatient care; after an admission: complication controlled, medicines and surveillance dates clear
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review every 6 months with ultrasound, MELD and medicine check; sooner after any decompensation (NICE).

algorithms.title: Staging and surveillance after a diagnosis of cirrhosis

nodes.text: Cirrhosis diagnosed or suspected
nodes.detail: Treat the cause and refer to hepatology.

nodes.text: Start HCC surveillance: ultrasound with or without AFP every 6 months
Is CSPH likely? (liver stiffness 25 kPa or more, or varices already seen)
Start carvedilol (or propranolol); no screening endoscopy needed
nodes.detail: Reduce if systolic BP below 90 mmHg.

nodes.text: Stiffness below 20 kPa AND platelets above 150 × 10⁹/L?
No screening endoscopy; repeat elastography and platelets yearly
Upper GI endoscopy
Medium or large varices?
Carvedilol or propranolol; band ligation if beta-blocker not tolerated
Repeat endoscopy every 3 years (2 if disease active, yearly if decompensated)

algorithms.title: Each follow-up visit: compensated or decompensated?

nodes.text: Follow-up visit for cirrhosis
Any decompensation? (ascites, bleeding, encephalopathy, jaundice)
Compensated: treat cause, beta-blocker if CSPH, 6-monthly ultrasound and MELD
Which complication?
Diagnostic tap; salt restriction; spironolactone with or without furosemide
High SBP risk? (protein 15 g/L or less, Child-Pugh above 9, MELD above 16, prior SBP)
Norfloxacin or ciprofloxacin prophylaxis; transplant referral
No routine prophylaxis; review diuretic response and kidneys
Find the trigger (infection, bleeding, constipation, sedatives, low sodium)
Lactulose to 2–3 soft stools; add rifaximin after a recurrence; refer
Emergency: resuscitate, vasoactive drug, antibiotics, endoscopy (Upper GI bleeding topic)
Look for alcohol relapse, drugs, viral flare or HCC; refer for transplant assessment
